To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(1) radiation diffuses over the length and time scales of fluctuations in MRI-driven turbulence, (2) radiation is locked to the gas when it diffuses less than a turbulent vertical wavelength, and (3) MRI-driven turbulence can drive a disk to the marginally stable state.

(a) MRI in radiation-dominated accretion disks leads to turbulence, and (b) radiation pressure is more effective in resisting squeezing when radiation diffuses over the length and time scales of the turbulence.

(i) radiation pressure is less important in resisting squeezing when radiation diffuses over a distance that is similar to the vertical size of MRI fluctuations and (ii) MRI-driven turbulent stresses in radiation-dominated accretion disks are approximately proportional to the magnetic energy density, independent of opacity.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of radiation pressure on the dynamics of magnetized accretion disks.

the dynamics of the inner region of accretion disks around black holes, where radiation pressure is important, and the effects of radiation on the magnetohydrodynamic turbulence that is responsible for angular momentum transport.
the dynamics of the innermost parts of accretion disks, which are likely to be dominated by magnetic stresses and radiation pressure.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the radiation pressure is a source of support for MRI turbulence, and the radiation pressure gradient is a source of stress, but the radiation pressure gradient also provides a sink for energy dissipated by the MRI.
radiation pressure is not as effective as gas pressure at resisting squeezing when radiation diffusion is comparable to the scale of MRI fluctuations.
the MRI in radiation-dominated disks is a robust mechanism that can drive turbulence and transport angular momentum.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
radiation is not a significant factor in the MRI, but it is a significant factor in its effects on the disk structure.
radiation pressure is as effective as gas pressure in resisting compression in MRI turbulence.
MRI turbulence is robust in radiation-dominated accretion disks, and the stress is independent of the radiation transport mechanism.
The main takeaway from our work is that
radiation pressure is effective in resisting squeezing in the absence of MRI.
radiation pressure can be effective at suppressing density fluctuations and associated dissipation in MRI turbulence when it is locked to the gas.
the dynamics of radiation-dominated disks are similar to those of the corresponding gas-dominated systems.
